title: A Shilling to Loughborough: Thomas Cook's First Excursion Train
dek: On a walk to a temperance meeting in June 1841, a Market Harborough wood-turner thought of hiring a train, and a month later several hundred people rode it.

story.event: Organising a temperance railway excursion from Leicester to Loughborough
story.summary: On 9 June 1841 Thomas Cook, a wood-turner and temperance campaigner in Market Harborough, conceived of a special train while walking to a temperance meeting in Leicester; the Midland Counties Railway's secretary agreed to provide one. On 5 July 1841 between 485 and 570 people, by differing counts, travelled from Leicester to a temperance gathering at Loughborough and back for a shilling each. Cook's later trips earned him little until his first profit-making excursion in 1845, and the firm that grew from them lasted until 2019.
paragraphs: On 9 June 1841, Thomas Cook, a 32-year-old wood-turner and Baptist preacher in Market Harborough, walked fifteen miles to Leicester for a temperance meeting. He was secretary of a local temperance association and printed anti-drink pamphlets at his own risk. On the way, according to his firm's 1891 history, he read a newspaper account of the new Midland Counties Railway. Cook later recalled the moment: "A thought flashed through my brain." Could the railway carry Leicester's temperance supporters to a rally planned at Loughborough?

What he knew of railways was thin. By his own account he had ridden only one short line, from Leicester out to a terminus near the collieries. That evening he put the idea to the meeting and asked those in favour to raise their hands; most did. He stayed in Leicester to see the railway's secretary, John Fox Bell, who, the firm's history says, replied: "I know nothing of you or your society, but you shall have the train." Bell also gave something towards the preliminary costs. Cook then went to Loughborough to arrange food for the marchers.

On 5 July 1841 the train left Leicester's Campbell Street station, its passengers in open carriages, a band having led them to the station. The fare, there and back, was a shilling. How many went depends on whom you read: 485 by the count Leicester's museums use, nearly 500 by Leicestershire County Council's, 570 in the firm's own 1891 history. Crowds met them at Loughborough, and after speeches, games and tea in a park they were back in Leicester at half past ten that night. Cook's seven-year-old son, John Mason Cook, was aboard.

It is often called the first publicly advertised excursion train in England, though members-only outings had run earlier. Over the next three summers Cook arranged more trips for temperance societies and Sunday schools, but they earned him little beyond the printing of posters and handbills; his first excursion run for profit came in 1845. By the end of 1841, his firm's history says, he had seen that his life would not go the way he had planned. The company that grew from that shilling fare lasted 178 years, until its collapse in 2019.

quote.text: Follow thine heart during thy lifetime; do not more than is commanded thee. Diminish not the time of following the heart; it is abhorred of the soul, that its time [of ease] be taken away.
quote.work: The Instruction of Ptahhotep (and of Ke'gemni)
quote.source_title: The Instruction of Ptah-Hotep and the Instruction of Ke'Gemni, tr. Battiscombe G. Gunn, Project Gutenberg eBook #30508
quote.connection: Cook's train was a campaign, meant to draw people away from drink and the races. Ptahhotep, a vizier instructing his son, defends ease for its own sake. The day at Loughborough, with its band, games and tea, was a demonstration and a holiday at once, and the maxim asks that the holiday be taken seriously too.

reflection: Cook did not need to understand railways to see what a train could do. He knew his own people and their meeting, and he went and asked the man who did understand railways. That man said yes to someone he had never heard of.

There is a second thing in that day out. Several hundred people spent it on music, games and tea, and came home late. You may be carrying a serious purpose of your own, the kind that makes a free afternoon feel like a lapse. Ptahhotep would say the afternoon belongs to the purpose rather than being stolen from it.
invitation: Choose one hour this week that belongs to no cause, not even a good one. Put it in your calendar today, and tell someone at home when it is.

research_notes: Passenger numbers disagree and the story gives all three with their sources: 485 (Leicester Museums and Leicester City Council's Story of Leicester), nearly 500 tickets (Leicestershire County Council, 2023) and 570 (W. Fraser Rae's 1891 company history and the 1892 Railroad News obituary). The Internet Archive text of Fraser Rae prints '670 passengers' once on page 22 but '570 passengers' and 'upwards of five hundred and seventy' on pages 24 and 27; the 670 is treated as a misprint or scanning error. The full text is at https://archive.org/download/cu31924011771668/cu31924011771668_djvu.txt. Fraser Rae's book was published by Thomas Cook & Son for the firm's jubilee and is partial to Cook; details that rest on it alone (the show of hands, John Fox Bell's reply and contribution, Cook's limited railway experience, his realisation at the end of 1841) are attributed to 'his firm's history' or 'his own account'. The 'A thought flashed through my brain' line is Cook's own later recollection as quoted by Leicester City Council; the rest of that sentence is longer than 25 words and is not used. Date of the idea: Fraser Rae and Story of Leicester give the walk as 9 June 1841; Leicestershire County Council says Cook 'hit upon the idea' in July, which conflicts and is not followed. Railway: in 1841 the line was the Midland Counties Railway (Leicestershire County Council, Leicester Museums, Fraser Rae); Story of Leicester's 'Midland Railway Company' is anachronistic, since the Midland Railway was formed in 1844. Distance (11 or 12 miles) varies and is not given. Leicester Museums describe the party as members of Cook's Baptist church, others as temperance supporters; the story follows the temperance account given by most sources. 'First' claim: Fraser Rae concedes that members-only Mechanics' Institute trains ran before Cook's, so the story says 'often called the first publicly advertised excursion train in England'. Cook's age: born 22 November 1808 (obituary), so 32 in June 1841. Funding: Cook organised the trip himself with no investors; Bell's contribution towards preliminary expenses is mentioned. Industry given as travel and tourism rather than the slate's hospitality. The Ptahhotep maxim is from a vizier's instruction to his son and is applied here by analogy; the brackets around 'of ease' are Gunn's.
